title: Sleep, Cortisol & Visible Depletion
hook: A tired face is read as sad and unwell, and a tired reader sees more threat in others; sleep shapes both sides of every look.
why:
Every reading in this book happens between two bodies, and both of them have slept well or badly, eaten or not, and are at some point in their daily rhythm. These states change how a face looks, how a voice sounds and how a reader interprets what he sees. They are among the most common causes of misreading there are, and among the most ignored.

This chapter is about depletion: what sleep loss does to how people look, how it changes the way a tired reader sees others, how the body's daily rhythm shifts alertness and mood, how hunger turns up the dial on irritation, and how all of these shift a person's baseline. It ends with the simplest discipline in the book: check your own tank before you read anyone, and offer others rest and food before you judge them. When poor sleep is chronic, the chapter also says when to see a doctor, because some sleep problems are treatable conditions.

teach.h: Sleep loss is written on the face.
teach.p:
In 2013 Tina Sundelin and colleagues photographed ten people twice: once after a normal night's sleep, and once after about thirty-one hours without sleep. Observers who did not know which was which rated the photographs. After sleep deprivation, faces were judged to have more hanging eyelids, redder and more swollen eyes, darker circles under the eyes, paler skin and more drooping corners of the mouth. They were also judged to look sadder. A related study by John Axelsson and colleagues in 2010 found that sleep-deprived faces were rated less healthy and less attractive.

Later work using objective measurements found the picture more mixed, but confirmed that features such as less open eyes, a downturned mouth and darker skin around the eyes made faces look more tired to others. The face plate here shows the lids at rest, tightened and raised; sleep loss tends to lower and narrow them, as if the face were slowly closing.

For a reader, the important point is the overlap. Drooping lids, a downturned mouth and a flat expression are also the features people read as sadness, boredom, low mood or disapproval. A tired face and a sad face can look almost the same.

So when a colleague arrives looking flat, heavy-lidded and down-turned, the first rival to consider is not their mood but their night. New parents, shift workers, carers, students before exams, people with chronic pain and people with insomnia often look like this for reasons that have nothing to do with how they feel about you, their work or their life.

Before you read a mood in a face, ask how the face slept.
teach.disconfirm: If sleep-deprived faces were rated no differently from rested ones, sleep would not need to be on your list of rivals. The studies described here found clear differences in how tired and how sad people looked.

teach.h: Tired faces are read as moods.
teach.p:
The overlap between tired and sad faces has practical consequences that most people never think about. A man who arrives at a job interview after a sleepless night may be read as unenthusiastic. A teacher may read a pupil's heavy eyes as boredom when the pupil was up half the night caring for a younger sibling. A partner may take a tired face at breakfast as a sign of resentment. A manager may decide that a new father has lost interest in his work.

Tiredness also changes behaviour in ways that look like mood. Tired people speak more slowly and with less variation, move less, smile less, respond more slowly, and are more easily irritated. The chapter on depression's physical signature described similar changes in low mood, which is one more reason why none of those signs can diagnose anything.

The correction is to read against the person's baseline and circumstances, as always. Do you know how they have been sleeping? Is there a new baby, a sick parent, a night shift, an exam, a bereavement? Is this how they look every Monday, or every afternoon? A face that looks flat once is weather. A face that has looked flat for weeks may be climate, and may deserve a question about sleep and how things are.

Asking about sleep is also one of the easiest ways into a harder conversation. *You look shattered. How are you sleeping?* is a question almost anyone can answer, and the answer often opens onto whatever is keeping them awake.

Many of the moods you read in the morning are really nights you did not see.
teach.disconfirm: If people's expressions and movements stayed the same whether they had slept well or badly, tiredness could not be mistaken for mood. Most people can recall a time when their own tiredness was taken for something else.
teach.pullQuote: Many of the moods you read in the morning are really nights you did not see.

teach.h: A tired brain sees more threat.
teach.p:
Sleep loss does not only change how you look. It changes how you see. In 2015 Andrea Goldstein-Piekarski, Matthew Walker and colleagues showed eighteen young adults a series of faces ranging from friendly to threatening, once after a normal night's sleep and once after twenty-four hours awake, while recording their brain activity and heart responses. After sleep deprivation, their brains and hearts distinguished less clearly between friendly and threatening faces, and they rated more faces as threatening, including ones that were friendly or neutral.

This has direct consequences for everything else in this book. A reader who has slept badly is more likely to read a colleague's neutral face as hostile, a partner's question as an attack, a stranger's glance as a challenge. The chapter on reading yourself under stress in Part VI described how stress biases readings towards threat; sleep loss does something similar, and the two often come together.

It also helps explain the irritability that comes with tiredness. A tired person is not only shorter of patience; they are seeing more provocation in the world around them. What feels like reacting to other people's hostility may partly be reacting to their own depleted perception.

The practical rule is simple. When you have slept badly, hold your readings of other people more lightly, especially readings of hostility, rejection or threat. Tag them in your journal with your state, as the calibration chapter suggested, and recheck them after a good night. Many will soften.

A tired reader is a biased reader, in a predictable direction.
teach.disconfirm: If people's judgments of faces were just as accurate after a sleepless night as after a normal one, sleep loss would not bias reading. The study described here found a measurable shift towards seeing threat.

teach.h: The body's daily rhythm moves the baseline.
teach.p:
Even with good sleep, the body changes through the day. An internal clock, the circadian rhythm, shapes alertness, mood, body temperature and hormones over roughly twenty-four hours. Cortisol, the hormone involved in the stress response, normally rises sharply in the first half-hour or so after waking, helping the body get going, and falls through the rest of the day. Alertness tends to dip in the early afternoon and falls sharply in the small hours.

These rhythms differ between people. Some are larks, at their best early; some are owls, sharpest in the evening. Teenagers' clocks typically shift later, which is why many of them are genuinely unable to feel awake at eight in the morning and wide awake at midnight. Shift workers and people with jet lag are living out of step with their own clocks, which shows in their faces, their tempers and their judgment.

For a reader, this means that the same person has different baselines at different times of day. The colleague who is lively at ten may be flat at three, and neither is unusual for him. The teenager who grunts at breakfast may talk freely at ten at night. Reading the afternoon slump as disinterest, or the morning grunt as rudeness, is a timing error.

It also suggests when to hold important conversations. Where you can choose, avoid the low points of the day for both of you. A difficult conversation at four in the afternoon, at the end of a long day, often goes worse than the same conversation at eleven in the morning.
teach.disconfirm: If people's mood, alertness and patience stayed the same at all times of day, timing would not matter. Most people can identify their own best and worst hours, and the research on circadian rhythms describes why.

teach.p:
Most people have heard of being *hangry*. In research published in 2018 and 2019, Jennifer MacCormack and Kristen Lindquist examined what is actually going on. In their studies, hunger on its own did not make people more negative. But when hungry people were placed in a negative context, for example shown an unpleasant image before judging something ambiguous, or treated unfairly by a researcher, they judged things more harshly and reported more negative feelings than people who had eaten. Hungry people who had first been asked to pay attention to their own feelings showed less of this effect.

Hunger, in other words, turns up the dial on whatever is already going on. In a pleasant situation it may hardly show. In a tense meeting, an argument or a frustrating day, it can tip ordinary irritation into anger, and the person may blame the situation entirely, not noticing that their body is low on fuel.

For a reader, this adds another rival explanation for irritability, impatience and harsh judgments, in others and in yourself. It is one reason why long meetings without food go badly in their last hour, why family arguments cluster before dinner, and why a man who skipped lunch reads his manager's email as an insult.

The response is simple and old-fashioned. Feed people before difficult conversations. Notice when you are hungry before you judge anyone. And, as the study suggests, naming the feeling helps: *I'm hungry and I'm reading this badly* is often enough to turn the dial back down.

Before you decide someone is being unreasonable, check whether either of you has eaten.
teach.disconfirm: If hungry people in negative situations judged things no more harshly than fed people, hunger would not need to be on your list of rivals. The studies described here found that it did, especially when people were not attending to their own feelings.

teach.p:
Sleep loss, hunger, the time of day, thirst, illness, pain and long hours all combine, and together they can shift a person's baseline a long way from where you would usually expect it. A nurse at the end of a twelve-hour night shift, a lorry driver after ten hours on the road, a father on the third night of a teething baby, a man with a migraine: each will look, sound and react differently from their rested self, and none of it is about you.

This is why the journal described in Part VI begins every entry with a line about your own state, and why it is worth adding what you know of the other person's state too. A reading of someone at the end of a double shift should be filed differently from a reading of the same person after a holiday.

It is also why depletion is so easily missed in people who are depleted all the time. Someone with a newborn, a long-term caring role, chronic pain or a demanding job may have been running on a shifted baseline for months. The chapter on the stress posture described how chronic stress hides in the slow drift of a baseline; chronic depletion hides the same way. Comparing with how they were a year ago, not last week, shows the change.

When you notice that someone is depleted, the most useful response is often practical rather than conversational. Offer food, water, a seat, a break, a lift home, the chance to take the hard conversation another day. These do more than any reading.

Depletion is the most ordinary explanation there is, and the one most often forgotten.
teach.disconfirm: If depleted people looked and behaved just like rested ones, depletion would not shift the baseline. Most people can see the difference in themselves at the end of a very long day.

teach.h: Check your own tank, and know when to see a doctor.
teach.p:
Every chapter in this book starts with reading yourself, and depletion is where that matters most, because it biases readings in predictable ways. Before an important reading, a hard conversation or a judgment about someone, run a quick check. How did I sleep? When did I last eat? What time is it, and am I at a high or a low point? Am I in pain, ill, dehydrated? If the answers are poor, and the matter can wait, let it wait. If it cannot, hold your readings more lightly and say so to yourself.

Do the same for others. When someone seems hostile, flat, irritable or uninterested, ask whether they are tired, hungry or at the end of a long day before you ask anything about their character or their feelings towards you.

And know when tiredness is more than a bad week. Persistent difficulty getting to sleep or staying asleep, over months, is common and treatable; a structured talking therapy for insomnia is recommended in many countries as the first treatment, ahead of sleeping tablets. Loud snoring, pauses in breathing or gasping during sleep, and heavy daytime sleepiness can be signs of sleep apnoea, which is also treatable and worth taking seriously, especially for anyone who drives. Long-term exhaustion can also come from physical conditions such as anaemia or thyroid problems. In each case, the right step is a doctor's appointment.

Persistent sleep problems also go with low mood and anxiety, as earlier chapters in this part described. If a person's sleep has collapsed alongside hopelessness or withdrawal, it is a reason to ask more, and to help them reach help.
teach.disconfirm: If checking your own sleep, food and timing before important readings made those readings no more accurate, the habit would add nothing. Tag a month of readings with your state and compare, as the calibration chapter suggested.

caseStudy:
Mark, thirty-five, manages a small sales team. In March his daughter is born, and for the next two months he sleeps in two- and three-hour pieces. He keeps working full days. In the Monday meetings, he finds his team difficult. One junior, Priya, seems to look at him with contempt whenever he speaks. In April he snaps at her in front of everyone for what he reads as an eye-roll.

That evening his partner says, gently, that he has been snapping at her too, and that he looks terrible. Mark thinks about it. He realises that every Monday meeting has come after the worst night of the week, since his partner works Sunday nights and he does the night feeds alone. He has been reading faces through two hours' sleep.

He makes three changes. He moves the team meeting from nine on Monday to eleven on Tuesday, after the better night and a proper breakfast. He starts noting his sleep in the top line of his journal, and holds any reading of a colleague as hostile, on a short-sleep day, until he has slept on it. And he apologises to Priya, privately, telling her honestly that he has been running on very little sleep and that he took it out on her.

Priya tells him that she had been rubbing her eyes because she had an eye infection, and had been worried all week that he was going to sack her.

By June the baby sleeps longer. Mark notices that the team has become, as he puts it, much nicer. He suspects most of the change was in him.
observe: Notice someone who looks flat or down today, and consider what you know about how they have been sleeping.
Notice your own readings of other people on a day after poor sleep, and whether more of them lean towards hostility.
Notice the time of day and whether people have eaten, the next time a meeting or conversation turns tense.

drills.name: State Line
steps: For two weeks, start each journal entry with your hours of sleep, when you last ate, and the time of day.
Tag any reading of another person as hostile, rejecting or threatening.
At the end of the fortnight, compare how many such readings you made on short-sleep days and on rested days.
Check any that you were later able to confirm or refute.
Write one sentence about how depletion affects your reading.
variations: Add a line for what you ate and when, and see whether hunger changes your readings as much as sleep does.
Ask someone you live with to rate your mood each evening for a week, and compare their ratings with your sleep.

drills.name: Best Hours
steps: Write down, for yourself, the times of day when you feel sharpest and when you feel flattest.
Do the same, from observation, for two people you work or live with.
Note when your hardest conversations with each of them usually happen.
Identify one conversation you could move to a better time for both of you.
Move it, and note any difference.
variations: Ask the two people directly when they feel sharpest, and compare their answers with your observations.
Choose one recurring meeting and suggest moving it to a better time for most of the people in it.

drills.name: Feed First
steps: Before your next difficult meeting or conversation, make sure you have eaten and had water.
If you can, offer food or a drink to the other person too.
Notice how the conversation goes compared with similar ones in the past.
Notice whether you felt the urge to judge harshly at any point.
Write down whether you will make this a habit.
variations: Try having a snack before a difficult email as well as before a meeting, and notice whether it changes your tone.
Notice for a week how often difficult conversations at home happen before dinner, and try moving one.

drills.name: Sleep Question
steps: Choose someone who has looked flat or tired lately.
Ask them, simply, how they have been sleeping.
Listen to the answer without offering advice.
If the answer opens onto something harder, follow it with a curious question.
Note what you learned that you would not have learned by reading their face.
variations: Ask the sleep question of someone you see only occasionally, and notice how much it changes your reading of them.
Ask yourself the same question each morning for a week before you judge anyone else's mood.

drills.name: Know the Signs
steps: Write down the signs in this chapter that suggest a sleep problem worth seeing a doctor about.
Ask yourself honestly whether any apply to you.
Ask your partner or housemate, if you have one, whether you snore loudly or seem to stop breathing at night.
If any signs apply, write down how you would book a doctor's appointment.
Book it, if needed, this week.
variations: Find out whether your workplace has a policy on rest breaks or night shifts, and what it says.
If you drive for work, write down where you would stop if you felt drowsy on your usual routes.

quiz.q: After a sleepless night, a colleague's face looks flat, heavy-lidded and turned down at the mouth. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That she is unhappy in her job and probably looking for another one
That she disapproves of you, and is showing it without saying so
That sleep loss itself makes faces look sad; ask about sleep before assuming mood
That she is depressed and should be encouraged to see a doctor today
quiz.explain: Sleep loss lowers the lids, darkens the eyes and turns the mouth down, and observers read sleep-deprived faces as sadder. Asking about the night is the first and easiest check before reading anything about her feelings.

quiz.q: What did Goldstein-Piekarski and colleagues find after people had gone a night without sleep?
options: People rated more faces as threatening, including friendly ones
People read faces more accurately because they were more alert to danger
People rated every face as friendly, failing to notice real threats
People's reading of faces did not change in any measurable way at all
quiz.explain: Sleep loss blurred the brain's and heart's distinction between friendly and threatening faces, and people saw more threat. A tired reader is biased towards hostility.

quiz.q: Which changes did Sundelin and colleagues find in faces after sleep deprivation?
options: Wider-open eyes and a fixed, alert stare, as if the person were on edge
Flushed cheeks and tense lips, as if the person were holding back anger
No visible changes at all, though the people reported feeling much more tired
Hanging lids, red or swollen eyes, dark circles, paler skin, drooping mouths
quiz.explain: Observers rated sleep-deprived faces as showing these changes and as looking sadder. Because the features overlap with sadness and boredom, tiredness is easily mistaken for mood.

quiz.q: You have to have a difficult conversation with a colleague. You slept badly and have not eaten since breakfast. What fits this chapter?
options: Go ahead straight away, since putting it off will only make it harder
If it can wait, move it to when you are rested and fed; if not, hold readings lightly
Have it, but keep it short so that your tiredness does not show
Ask a colleague to have the conversation for you, since you are not at your best today
quiz.explain: Sleep loss and hunger both bias you towards reading hostility and reacting harshly. Choosing a better time, or at least holding your readings lightly, protects both of you.

quiz.q: What did MacCormack and Lindquist find about hunger and judgment?
options: Hunger made people more negative in every situation, whatever the context
Hunger made people kinder, since they wanted others to share their food with them
Hungry people judged more harshly in negative contexts, unless aware of feelings
Hunger had no effect at all on how people judged others or situations
quiz.explain: Hunger turned up the dial on negative situations, and people who were attending to their own feelings showed less of the effect. Naming it, I'm hungry, helps turn it back down.

quiz.q: Your partner has woken exhausted for months, snores loudly and sometimes seems to stop breathing at night. What fits this chapter?
options: Encourage a doctor's appointment, since these can be signs of a treatable condition
Suggest an earlier bedtime, since the exhaustion is just from a lack of sleep
Buy earplugs for yourself, since the snoring is the only real problem here
Wait to see whether it improves on the next holiday before doing anything
quiz.explain: Loud snoring, pauses in breathing and heavy daytime tiredness can be signs of sleep apnoea, which is treatable and important, especially for drivers. A doctor can assess it.

quiz.q: In Sundelin and colleagues' study, how long had people gone without sleep before the second photograph was taken?
options: About thirty-one hours
About three hours, after a short afternoon nap
About a week, with only very brief naps allowed
About one hundred hours, under constant medical supervision
quiz.explain: Participants were photographed after a normal night and again after about thirty-one hours without sleep. Observers rated the sleep-deprived faces as more tired-looking and also sadder.

quiz.q: A thirteen-year-old keeps falling asleep in class, arrives late with red, heavy eyes and once brought someone else's prescription to school. A colleague wants to give her detentions. What fits this chapter best?
options: Give her detentions until she learns to go to bed at a sensible time
Tell her parents she is clearly on her phone all night and needs stricter rules
Ask her privately how she is sleeping and whether things are all right at home
Move her to the front of the class so that she cannot fall asleep
quiz.explain: Her face shows exhaustion but not its cause. A private, kind question can uncover reasons such as caring for someone at home, which a detention would never reach.

quiz.q: Someone cites the 2011 study of Israeli parole judges as proof that hungry judges are much harsher. What does this chapter say?
options: It is proof, since the study has been replicated in every country since
The study has been strongly questioned; case order may explain the pattern
It is proof, but only for judges who skip breakfast before court
It shows that judges are kinder when they are hungry, not harsher
quiz.explain: Critics pointed out that cases were not heard in random order, which could produce the pattern on its own. Better-controlled studies suggest hunger can harshen judgments in negative or ambiguous situations.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific time when you misread someone, or were misread, and tiredness or hunger played a part: a flat face taken for a mood, an irritable exchange before a meal, a sharp judgment after a bad night. Describe the state of both bodies at the time, as well as you can. How did the depletion shape what was seen and how it was interpreted? What will you check, in yourself and in the other person, the next time a conversation that matters falls on a depleted day?
reflection.guidance: Most people find that depletion was a factor in more of their misreadings than they had realised, and that it is rarely mentioned at the time. Be specific about sleep, food and time of day. The check you write at the end should be quick enough to actually use: three questions you can ask yourself in ten seconds.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read tiredness as a mood, deciding that a flat, heavy-lidded face is sad, bored or disapproving when it is simply short of sleep. The second is to forget that you are tired too, and to trust readings made after a bad night, which lean towards seeing threat. The third is to ignore timing and hunger, holding hard conversations at the low point of the day with nobody fed. The fourth is to miss chronic depletion in people who have been running on empty for months. And the fifth is to treat persistent sleep problems as a fact of life when they may be treatable conditions, such as insomnia or sleep apnoea. Check your own tank, ask about the other person's, offer rest and food before judgment, and see a doctor when tiredness will not lift.

moreCases.title: The girl who slept in maths
moreCases.scene:
Mr Okafor teaches maths at a comprehensive school. Kayleigh, thirteen, sits near the back of his Year 8 class. Since the autumn she has
  started arriving late to the first lesson, her hair unbrushed, her eyes red and heavy-lidded. She yawns constantly, rests her head on her arm
  and twice has fallen asleep at her desk. Her homework is often missing. When he asks her a question, she looks up slowly, as if from a long way
  away, and says she does not know.

  Another teacher tells Mr Okafor that Kayleigh is "on her phone all night like the rest of them" and needs a detention or two to sort her out.
  Mr Okafor gave her one in October. It made no difference, and Kayleigh did not argue or complain about it, which struck him as odd for a
  thirteen-year-old.

  One morning, he notices that she has a carrier bag of shopping with her, and that she is carrying a box of prescription medication with someone
  else's name on it.

Kayleigh has also stopped going to the after-school netball club, which she joined in Year 7, and she eats her lunch quickly, alone, and spends the rest of the break with her head down on a table in the library.

When Mr Okafor looks back through his register, he finds that Kayleigh's lateness started in the week after October half-term, and that she has been late on almost every Monday and Thursday since.
moreCases.misread:
The other teacher read Kayleigh's heavy eyes, yawns and sleeping in class as laziness or late-night phone use, and the detention treated tiredness as a discipline problem. Neither reading asked why a thirteen-year-old might be so short of sleep.

And because Kayleigh accepted the detention without complaint, the teachers took her silence as indifference, when it may have been the exhaustion of a child who had no energy left to argue.

The detention also sent a message that the school had noticed her tiredness and decided it was her fault, which made it less likely that she would ever explain it.

The comment about the phone was also an assumption about her generation rather than about her, which made it easy to believe and impossible to check without asking.
moreCases.betterRead:
Sundelin's research showed how clearly sleep loss is written on the face: hanging eyelids, red and swollen eyes, paler skin and a mouth that droops, which observers also read as sadness. Kayleigh's face told Mr Okafor that she was exhausted. It did not tell him why. The shopping and the medication suggested a possibility that the detention had ignored: that she might be a young carer, looking after someone at home. Mr Okafor's better approach was to ask, privately and kindly, at the end of the lesson: "You look really tired lately. Is everything all right at home?" Kayleigh said that her mum had multiple sclerosis and that she got up in the night to help her, and did the shopping before school. Mr Okafor told her she had done nothing wrong, thanked her for telling him, and passed it on, with her permission, to the school's pastoral lead, who arranged support from the local young carers' service and a quiet word with her other teachers.

He also stopped giving detentions for lateness to that class without first asking why, which surfaced one more pupil who was caring for a grandparent.

moreCases.title: The mother who saw criticism everywhere
moreCases.scene:
Hannah, thirty-two, has a three-month-old son who wakes every two hours. Her husband works long shifts, and most nights she is up alone.
  Her mother-in-law, Margaret, visits three times a week to help. Hannah has started to dread the visits. She is sure Margaret disapproves of
  her. When Margaret picks up the baby, Hannah sees a tightening of the mouth that she reads as a judgment of how she has dressed him. When
  Margaret asks whether he has been fed, Hannah hears an accusation. When Margaret is quiet, Hannah reads the silence as disapproval.

  One afternoon, when Margaret suggests that Hannah lie down for an hour while she watches the baby, Hannah bursts into tears and tells her that
  she knows she thinks she is a terrible mother.

  Margaret is stunned. She tells Hannah that she thinks she is doing an amazing job, and that she has been worried about her because she looks so
  exhausted.

Hannah's husband has also noticed that she cries more easily, that she is snapping at him over small things, and that she has stopped seeing her friends from her antenatal group. He has put it down to tiredness and hopes it will pass.

Margaret, for her part, has been holding back. She remembers her own mother-in-law, who criticised everything, and she has promised herself never to be like her. So she says very little, watches carefully, and asks only the questions she thinks a helpful grandmother should ask. The more carefully she watches, the more Hannah feels watched.
moreCases.misread:
Hannah read Margaret's neutral faces, ordinary questions and silences as criticism. Her own exhaustion was colouring every reading, so that ambiguous signals looked hostile, and she did not consider that the hostility might be in her reading rather than in Margaret.

She also did not notice that her readings were worst in the late afternoon, after the longest stretch since she had slept, and best on the rare mornings after a better night.

And because she read every visit as an inspection, she began to perform for Margaret, tidying and dressing the baby before she arrived, which made her more exhausted still.
moreCases.betterRead:
Goldstein-Piekarski, Walker and colleagues found that after a night without sleep, people's brains and bodies distinguished less clearly between friendly and threatening faces, and they judged more faces as threatening, including neutral ones. Months of broken sleep with a new baby can have a similar effect on a reader: ambiguous signals tip towards threat, and a mother-in-law's tight mouth becomes a verdict. Hannah's better reading came once Margaret's words had broken through. They talked, and agreed that Margaret would take the baby for one long nap a day while Hannah slept, with no discussion of feeds or clothes unless Hannah asked. A few weeks of better sleep later, Hannah found that the tight mouth she had dreaded was simply how Margaret concentrated, and that she made the same face doing the crossword. She also mentioned to her health visitor how low and tearful she had been feeling, which the health visitor took seriously and followed up.

Margaret, for her part, started saying aloud what she was thinking, "He looks lovely in that," so that Hannah did not have to guess.

moreCases.title: The date after the night shift
moreCases.scene:
Leon, thirty, is a paramedic. He has arranged a first date with Abi, whom he met through a friend, for a Saturday lunchtime. On the
  Friday night, his ambulance is called out to a serious crash, and his shift ends three hours late. He has slept for two hours when he meets Abi
  at the café.

  Abi finds him hard to read. His eyelids are heavy, his face is pale and flat, and he smiles only briefly. He listens, but slowly, and twice asks
  her to repeat something. His voice is lower and quieter than it was on the phone. Halfway through lunch he yawns, then apologises. Abi decides
  that he is bored, or that he does not find her interesting, and begins to wrap up the conversation early.

  As they leave, Leon says he is really sorry he has been such poor company, and that he came off a night shift at nine that morning after a bad
  job, and nearly cancelled but did not want to let her down.

Abi has been on several disappointing dates this year and has started to expect them to go badly. When Leon yawns, it feels like confirmation of something she already believed would happen.

Leon has also not eaten since a cereal bar at three in the morning. He orders a large breakfast at lunchtime, which Abi notices and finds slightly odd, and eats it quickly, without saying much.
moreCases.misread:
Abi read Leon's heavy eyelids, flat face, slow responses and yawn as boredom or lack of interest in her. She read his tiredness as a feeling about her, because that was what the date was about.

Her own expectation also shaped the reading. A reader who expects to be rejected finds rejection in ambiguous faces more easily, especially faces she has no baseline for.

Leon, for his part, misread the date too. He saw her wrapping up early as a sign that she had decided against him, and nearly did not apologise at all.
moreCases.betterRead:
Faces after sleep loss look sadder and less engaged, and the behaviours that come with tiredness, slower responses, missed words, flat speech and yawning, overlap almost exactly with the signs of boredom. A reader who does not know someone's sleep has little way of telling the two apart. Abi had no baseline for Leon, which made the misreading easy, and his apology changed everything. Her better reading was that she had met an exhausted man who had made an effort to keep his word, which said rather more about him than his eyelids had. She told him she was glad he had not cancelled, and suggested they try again the following weekend, when he had slept. On the second date, rested, he was animated, funny and asked her more questions than anyone had in months.

Abi said later that his apology at the door was the moment she started to like him. It was the first thing all afternoon that had not been filtered through his exhaustion.

moreCases.title: The argument before dinner
moreCases.scene:
Sophie and James, both in their thirties, have been meaning to talk about money for weeks: whether they can afford a bigger flat, and
  how to split their savings. They finally sit down to do it on a Thursday at seven in the evening, both straight from work. Neither has eaten
  since a sandwich at midday. James has had a difficult afternoon with a client.

  The conversation goes wrong almost at once. James's face looks tight and impatient to Sophie, and she reads his question about her spending as
  an accusation. Sophie's sigh, when he shows her a spreadsheet, looks to James like contempt. Within twenty minutes they are both speaking sharply,
  and Sophie says something about his mother's money that she instantly regrets. James walks out to the kitchen and starts making pasta, banging
  the pans.

  Over the pasta, neither of them says much. By the end of the meal, both are calmer, and Sophie apologises.

They had planned the conversation for the weekend, then moved it to Thursday because Sophie's sister was visiting. Neither of them thought about how they would feel by seven on a Thursday.

Sophie has also had a bad week. Her manager told her on Tuesday that her team's budget would be cut, and she has been carrying the worry around ever since without mentioning it to James. When he opens the spreadsheet, all she can see is another set of numbers telling her she cannot have what she wants.

James, for his part, had prepared the spreadsheet carefully at lunchtime, colour-coded and annotated, and had been looking forward to showing it to Sophie as proof that they could afford the flat. Her sigh, to him, felt like a dismissal of the effort.
moreCases.misread:
Each of them read the other's face and tone as hostile, and each answered that hostility. Neither considered that both of them were hungry, tired and coming off a hard day, and that the evening had been set up for exactly this kind of misreading.

They also each read their own sharpness as a reaction to the other, rather than as a sign of their own hunger and fatigue, which is the hardest part of depletion to see from the inside.

The setting also mattered: across the kitchen table, facing each other over a laptop, in the posture of a negotiation rather than a conversation.

Neither of them was wrong to want the conversation. They were wrong only about when to have it.
moreCases.betterRead:
MacCormack and Lindquist found that hunger on its own did not make people more negative, but that hungry people in a negative or ambiguous situation judged things more harshly than people who had eaten. A money conversation at seven in the evening, after a long day, with neither person fed, is an ambiguous and loaded situation. Each tight face and each sigh was read through hunger and fatigue, and each harsh reading pushed the other one higher. Their better approach, which they agreed over the pasta, was to try again at a better time. They had the conversation on Saturday morning, after breakfast and a walk, with coffee on the table. It took an hour, they found that they mostly agreed, and James admitted that the spreadsheet had been a terrible way to start.

They also agreed a rule for the future: anything about money happens on a weekend morning, with breakfast first.

workedReading.title: The night handover
workedReading.scene:
Gloria is the day manager of a care home for older people. At seven each morning she takes handover from the night staff. This morning the night carer, Ade, who is usually warm and talkative, is short with her. He gives the handover in clipped sentences, does not smile, and when Gloria asks a follow-up question about one resident's fall, he says, "It's in the notes," and looks away. His face is grey, his eyes are red and he keeps rubbing his jaw. He has worked four twelve-hour nights in a row. Gloria feels a flash of irritation. She has had a difficult morning herself, with two staff off sick.

Gloria also knows that night staff often feel invisible to the day team, and that a brisk, critical handover can make them feel that their night's work counts for nothing.

Gloria knows Ade well. He has worked at the home for six years, mostly on nights by choice because it fits around his children's school day. He is the carer the residents ask for by name, and the one who sits with people who are dying when their families cannot be there.

steps.label: Check your own tank
steps.text:
Gloria starts with herself. She slept badly, worrying about the staffing, and has had nothing but coffee since she woke. She notes that she is at risk of reading Ade more harshly than he deserves, and that her irritation arrived very quickly, which is often a sign that the reader is depleted.

She also notes that she is at her own low point of the week: Monday morning, short-staffed, with a full day ahead. The conditions for a harsh reading could hardly be better.

She also has a quick biscuit from the tin in the office before she says anything else, which she notes is the first food she has eaten all day. It is a small thing, and it changes how much patience she has for the next ten minutes.

steps.label: Consider the hour and the shift
steps.text:
It is seven in the morning, at the end of a fourth consecutive night. Ade's body is at or near the low point of its daily rhythm, and he has been awake for most of the past twenty-four hours. That alone would change how anyone looked and spoke: heavier eyes, a flatter face, shorter answers, less patience.

She also remembers that the hours before dawn are when accidents and errors are most common in night work, and that a carer at the end of a run of nights deserves care himself.

She also reminds herself that she herself is short with people at the end of a long day, and that nobody who knows her takes it as a sign of what she really thinks of them.

steps.label: Compare with his baseline
steps.text:
On day shifts, and at the start of night shifts, Ade is one of the warmest members of staff, chatting with residents and joking with colleagues. Gloria has never seen him curt with anyone. Against that baseline, the change is large, and it lines up with the end of a long run of nights, not with anything she has done.

She also notes that she has rarely seen Ade at seven in the morning after four nights. Her baseline for him is mostly from day shifts, which is a reason to be cautious about comparing the two.

She also notes that Ade is quieter than usual with the residents who are up early, which suggests the change is in him, across the board, rather than in how he feels about her.

steps.label: Look at the cluster
steps.text:
The grey face, red eyes, jaw-rubbing, clipped speech and looking away all fit exhaustion, with a pacifier added. None of them is directed at her in particular. The one thing that might be about her is "It's in the notes", and even that fits a man who has written the notes carefully and has nothing left to explain them with.

She also notes what is missing: no complaint, no blame of anyone else, no carelessness in the written notes. A man annoyed with her would probably show it in more than one short sentence.

She also notices that he keeps glancing at the corridor where the resident who fell has her room. That is a clue she files for later: something about the fall may be on his mind.

steps.label: Hold the readings open
steps.text:
He may simply be exhausted. The fall may have been frightening and he may be worried about it. Something may have happened in the night that he has not mentioned. He may, less likely, be annoyed with her about the rota. Gloria notes that she does not need to know which right now, and that the handover is the wrong moment to find out.

She also decides not to raise the rota at handover, even though it is on her mind. One more topic, at the end of his fourth night, would be one more load.

Holding them open also stops her from saying the sentence that is forming in her head, about his tone, which would have been accurate and would have helped nobody.

steps.label: Adjust to the state
steps.text:
She keeps the rest of the handover short, reads the notes on the fall herself, and asks only the one question she needs answered for safety: whether the resident was seen by the doctor. Ade says yes. She thanks him, tells him he has done four long nights and should get home and sleep, and says she will ring him this afternoon if she has questions about the fall.

She also makes him a cup of tea before he goes, which takes two minutes and which Ade, she notices, holds with both hands as if it were the first warm thing he has touched all night.

She also asks the day nurse to check on the resident who fell straight away, so that Ade can go home knowing someone is looking after her.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
When Gloria rings at three, Ade answers sounding like himself. He apologises for being short and says that the fall had shaken him, because the resident had been on the floor for a few minutes before he found her, and he had been blaming himself all night. Gloria tells him he did everything right, and they talk it through properly. She also changes the rota so that no one works more than three nights in a row. She notes that her flash of irritation at seven in the morning would have produced a very different conversation.

She also starts asking night staff, at every handover, whether anything happened in the night that was hard for them, as well as what happened to the residents.

She also tells the rest of the day team, at the morning briefing, that the night had been hard, so that they read the night notes with that in mind.

moreFailures.title: Reading tiredness as a mood
moreFailures.body:
A tired face looks sad, flat, bored or disapproving, and tired behaviour, slower answers, shorter patience, less eye contact and less smiling, looks like a bad mood or a bad attitude. Without knowing how someone has slept, it is very easy to read their exhaustion as a feeling about you, the meeting or the conversation. The new father who seems uninterested at work, the pupil who seems bored, the date who seems disengaged, the partner who seems resentful at breakfast: each may simply be short of sleep. Before you decide what a flat face means, ask yourself what you know about the person's night, and if it matters, ask them.

It also helps to remember that tiredness can be invisible in conversation and obvious on camera. On video calls, under harsh light and at close range, a tired face can look even flatter than it does in person.

Parents of babies and young children, carers, shift workers and people with chronic pain are among those most often misread this way, because their tiredness is constant and rarely mentioned.

It also helps to give people the benefit of the doubt on Monday mornings and Friday afternoons, when the most people are tired, and to save judgments of anyone's mood for a time when they are more likely to be rested.

moreFailures.title: Trusting your own tired eyes
moreFailures.body:
Depletion changes the reader as well as the read. After poor sleep, people tend to see more threat in neutral faces, to judge more harshly, and to feel more irritable. A reading made at the end of a long day, after a bad night, on an empty stomach, is a reading made through a distorting lens. That does not mean it is wrong, but it does mean it deserves more checking than usual. If you notice yourself reading hostility everywhere on a tired day, it is worth asking whether the hostility is in the room or in you, and waiting until you are rested before acting on it, if you can.

It also helps to tell people when you are depleted. "I slept terribly, so if I seem short, it's not you" is a small sentence that can prevent a whole day of misreadings in both directions.

It also helps to separate a tired reading from a tired decision. You may not be able to stop yourself reading a colleague's face as hostile after a bad night, but you can stop yourself from sending the email you would write about it until the next day.

moreFailures.title: Holding hard conversations at the low point
moreFailures.body:
People often have difficult conversations at the worst possible times: late at night, at the end of a long day, before dinner, after a bad night's sleep, or in the early-afternoon dip. These are the times when both people are most likely to misread each other, to see threat, to answer harshly and to say things they regret. If a conversation matters and can wait, choose a time when both of you are rested and fed: late morning is often good. If it cannot wait, at least eat something, sit down, and agree to stop if it starts to go wrong.

Couples often find it helpful to agree a rule: no important decisions after ten at night or before food. It sounds trivial and it prevents a surprising number of rows.

At work, the same principle applies to scheduling. Difficult appraisals, disciplinary meetings and bad news are best delivered in the late morning, not at five on a Friday afternoon.

If you are a manager, it also helps to notice when your team's hardest meetings happen. A weekly meeting held at four o'clock on a Friday may be producing worse decisions every week without anyone realising why.

moreFailures.title: Treating constant exhaustion as normal
moreFailures.body:
Many people accept being tired all the time as part of modern life, and many men in particular push through exhaustion for years rather than mention it. Ordinary tiredness that comes from a busy week or a new baby usually improves with rest. Tiredness that does not, that lasts for months, or that comes with loud snoring and pauses in breathing at night, falling asleep during the day, difficulty sleeping most nights, low mood or other changes in health, deserves a conversation with a doctor. Many causes of persistent exhaustion, including sleep disorders, thyroid problems and anaemia, are treatable.

It also helps to notice when someone close to you seems to be falling asleep at odd times, such as in conversation or at the wheel. Raising it kindly can be the start of getting a treatable problem diagnosed.

It also helps to ask a partner or housemate what they notice about your sleep. People often have no idea that they snore, stop breathing or thrash about at night until someone tells them.

Men are often slower than women to see a doctor about tiredness, partly because it seems too ordinary to mention. It is not too ordinary. Persistent exhaustion is one of the commonest reasons doctors find treatable problems.

questions.q: How much sleep do adults need?
questions.a:
Most adults need at least seven hours a night on a regular basis, according to the consensus statement published in 2015 by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society, and many need more. Needs vary between people, and they change with age: teenagers need more than adults, and older adults often sleep more lightly. The best guide is how you feel. If you regularly need an alarm to drag you out of deep sleep, rely on caffeine to function, feel sleepy in the afternoon most days or sleep much longer at weekends, you are probably not getting enough.

It also helps to protect a regular wake time, even at weekends. Many sleep specialists find that a consistent time to get up does more for sleep than trying to go to bed earlier.

It also helps to know that caffeine can stay in the body for many hours, so an afternoon coffee may still be affecting sleep at bedtime, even in people who say it does not.

It also helps to treat sleep as part of reading well. A reader who protects his own sleep before an important day is doing something as useful as any amount of preparation.

questions.q: Can you tell from someone's face that they slept badly?
questions.a:
Sometimes. Sundelin and colleagues found that observers rated sleep-deprived faces as having more hanging eyelids, redder and more swollen eyes, darker circles, paler skin and more drooping corners of the mouth. But they also rated those faces as sadder, which shows the problem: the face of a tired person and the face of a sad person overlap a great deal. Make-up, lighting, skin tone, illness and age also change how a face looks. A tired-looking face is a reason to wonder about sleep, and to ask if it matters, rather than a reliable sign of it.

It may also help to know that people often underestimate how tired they look. If someone tells you that you look exhausted, it is usually worth taking seriously.

When you do ask, keep it light and specific: "Rough night?" or "How's the baby sleeping?" A question about sleep is one of the easiest ways into a conversation about how someone really is.

It also helps to be careful with comments about how someone looks. "You look tired" can land as "you look bad", especially for someone who is already struggling. A question about sleep is usually kinder than a comment about a face.

questions.q: Why does tiredness make me so irritable?
questions.a:
Partly because sleep loss affects the parts of the brain that help regulate emotion. Research by Matthew Walker's group and others has found that after sleep deprivation, people's emotional responses become stronger and less controlled, and, as Goldstein-Piekarski and colleagues found, people see more threat in neutral faces. A tired person has a shorter fuse, a stronger reaction to small annoyances and a greater tendency to read other people as hostile. Knowing this does not stop it happening, but it can help you notice it, and choose not to act on the first irritation of a tired day.

It also helps to have a plan for tired days: fewer important decisions, more patience with yourself, and an early night if you can manage one. A tired day is a bad day to judge anyone.

It also helps to apologise quickly when you snap on a tired day. A short, honest apology, "Sorry, I'm shattered, that wasn't about you," repairs most of the damage before it settles.

questions.q: Are judges really harsher before lunch?
questions.a:
A famous 2011 study by Shai Danziger and colleagues, of parole decisions by Israeli judges, reported that favourable rulings fell sharply as sessions went on and rose again after food breaks, and it is often quoted as proof that hunger affects judgment. The finding has been strongly questioned. Other researchers pointed out that the order of cases was not random, for example because prisoners without lawyers tended to be heard last in a session, and that this alone could produce the pattern. The safer conclusion comes from more controlled studies, such as MacCormack and Lindquist's: hunger can make judgments harsher in negative or ambiguous situations, which is reason enough to eat before a hard decision.

The story is a useful reminder that a vivid finding is not always a solid one. When a study seems to prove something neatly, it is worth asking whether anyone has checked it.

It also helps to apply the lesson to yourself. If you have an important decision to make about another person, such as a reference, a complaint or a hiring choice, make it when you are fed and rested, and look at it again the next day if you can.

No. People differ in their chronotype, the timing of their daily rhythm. Some are larks, alert early and tired by evening; others are owls, slow in the morning and at their best later in the day. These differences have a biological basis, and they shift with age: teenagers' rhythms move later, which is one reason so many struggle with early school starts, and older adults' rhythms often move earlier. An owl at a nine o'clock meeting may look sluggish and disengaged and be at their biological low point. Where you can, schedule important conversations at a time that suits both people's rhythms.

It also helps to know your own chronotype. If you are an owl, early meetings may show you at your worst, and it can be worth asking for later ones when they matter.

It also helps to be kind to teenagers who struggle in the morning. Their tiredness at an early start is often biology, not attitude, and treating it as laziness tends to make mornings worse.

Workplaces that allow flexible start times often find that owls do better work later in the day, and that the change costs little. It is worth asking about if mornings are your worst time.

When it does not go away with rest, when it lasts for weeks or months, or when it comes with other changes. Signs worth talking to a doctor about include loud snoring with pauses in breathing or gasping at night, which a partner may notice; feeling sleepy during the day despite enough time in bed; difficulty getting to sleep or staying asleep on most nights for months; and tiredness alongside low mood, weight change or other symptoms. And if you ever feel drowsy while driving, stop somewhere safe and rest. Sleepiness at the wheel is dangerous, and no deadline is worth it.

Shift workers deserve particular attention. Night shifts disrupt the body's rhythm, and people who work them for years often need extra support to sleep well and stay healthy.

It may also help to know that sleep problems and low mood often go together, each making the other worse. Treating one can help the other, which is one more reason to mention persistent sleep problems to a doctor.

And if someone you know seems to be struggling with sleep, offering practical help, such as taking a night feed, covering a shift or driving them home, can do more than any advice.

watch.title: Sleep Is Your Superpower
watch.notice: Matt Walker on what sleep loss does to the body and brain. Think about how it shows: the slowed face, the irritability, the poorer reading of other people's emotions.

reviewPrompt: This week, add your sleep and last meal to the top line of each journal entry, and hold any reading of hostility on a short-sleep day until you have slept.
